intro: Half of the Shepherd's Beech is lying on the ground, and both halves are still legally protected. Heavy icing broke its strongest limb in 2014; years later a whole side came down, weakened by a wood-decay fungus, and the standing half now leans on flexible bindings. It stands alone on open pasture at 807 metres near the hamlet of Lazy, came second in the national Tree of the Year vote in 2003, and by local legend grew overnight from a shepherd's staff.
meta_description: The Pastýřský buk near Lazy is half fallen and still protected, 5.88 metres round, second in the Czech Tree of the Year vote in 2003.
question_meta: The Pastýřský buk near Lazy is a storm-damaged, half-fallen beech, 5.88 metres round, roughly 200 to 280 years old.
question_answer: The Pastýřský buk (Shepherd's Beech) stands alone on open pasture near the hamlet of Lazy in the Slavkovský les, 5.88 metres round and estimated at roughly 200 to 280 years old. Half of it has fallen; both the standing and fallen sections remain protected.
question_context: The damage came in stages: heavy icing broke its strongest limb at the end of 2014, and some years later one whole side of the tree came down, likely weakened by the wood-decay fungus Kretzschmaria deusta, which blackens a trunk as if scorched. The standing half was stabilised with flexible bindings in the spring of 2015 and now stands tilted, while the fallen half has simply been left where it came down. In the autumn of 2003 it placed second in the Czech national Tree of the Year competition. Local legend has it growing overnight from a shepherd's staff planted in the ground during a storm, a story nobody claims to have witnessed. It stands alone on open grazing land at 807 metres elevation near the hamlet of Lazy in the Slavkovský les, free to reach on foot, with no public transport at the site itself. What makes it worth the walk is exactly this: a veteran left standing after the kind of damage that usually ends with a chainsaw.

trees.story:
Half of this beech is lying on the ground, and both halves are still legally protected. The standing part leans, held together with flexible bindings since the spring of 2015. The fallen part has been left where it came down.

It has been going wrong slowly. Heavy icing broke its strongest limb at the end of 2014. Some years later a whole side went over, helped along by Kretzschmaria deusta, a wood decay fungus that blackens a trunk until the tree looks as though it has been through a fire. Sources give the height as 22 metres or as 17, and the lower figure is almost certainly the tree as it is now. The trunk is 5.88 metres round and the crown once spread 21 metres across, which is what a beech does when it grows up alone with nothing to compete with. Nobody has dated it precisely; the estimates run from about 200 to 280 years.

That is where it stands, at 807 metres on the edge of the Lazy settlement in the Slavkovský les, out on open grazing land. In the autumn of 2003 it came second in the national Tree of the Year vote.

Local story has it growing from a shepherd's staff pushed into the ground during a storm, which sprouted overnight. Nobody claims to have watched.

best_time.label: October, when the last standing half turns copper on an open hillside

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a beech half fallen, the standing half leaning and bound with flexible strapping since 2015, its trunk blackened by decay fungus. It stands alone on open pastureland at 807m near Lazy.
